messages.author: 7d9d6983d8e204e0
messages.subject: Dealing with endogeneity in lavaan
parts:
Dear colleagues:

Consider the population model below, and the data that is created based on it with the function simulateData( ). Note that, due to the design of the population model, the latent variable CO is correlated with SU's residual, which leads to the issue of endogeneity.

mPopModel <- '  
# outer model
DM =~ DM1
CO =~ CO1
GT =~ 0.6*GT1 + 0.6*GT2 + 0.7*GT3 + 0.7*GT4 + 0.8*GT5
AC =~ 0.5*AC1 + 0.6*AC2 + 0.6*AC3 + 0.7*AC4 + 0.7*AC5
SU =~ 0.55*SU1 + 0.6*SU2 + 0.65*SU3 + 0.7*SU4 + 0.75*SU5
# inner model
DM ~ 0.0*CO
GT ~ 0.516*CO
AC ~ 0.288*CO
SU ~ 0.029*CO + 0.0*DM + 0.575*GT + 0.338*AC
'
mData_NORM <- simulateData(mPopModel,sample.nobs=10000L,std.lv=TRUE,standardized=TRUE)

Apparently running the SEM analysis below leads to incorrect estimations for the regressions, particularly for the following two regressions: GT ~ CO and AC ~ CO.

mModel <- '  
# outer model
DM =~ DM1
CO =~ CO1
GT =~ GT1 + GT2 + GT3 + GT4 + GT5
AC =~ AC1 + AC2 + AC3 + AC4 + AC5
SU =~ SU1 + SU2 + SU3 + SU4 + SU5
# inner model
DM ~ CO
GT ~ CO
AC ~ CO
SU ~ CO + DM + GT + AC
'
mFit_NORM <- sem(mModel,data=mData_NORM)
summary(mFit_NORM)

Running the analysis in two stages seems to solve the problem. That is, first including only DM ~ CO, GT ~ CO, and AC ~ CO; and then only SU ~ CO + DM + GT + AC.

However, I was wondering if there is a setting in lavaan that solves the problem, without my having to conduct a two-stage analysis.

Can anyone help?

Ned Kock

PS: If I use the Factor-Based PLS Type CFM1 algorithm in WarpPLS, the regressions (and other parameters) are correctly estimated in one single run, without the need for a two-stage analysis. This occurs in spite of endogeneity, which is clearly visible in the data.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Dealing with endogeneity in lavaan
parts:
I'm not sure what you think the problem is.  The structural model is a simple mediation model, albeit with 3 mediators instead of 1.  But the model parameters are all identified.  What "two stages" are you talking about?  I got parameter estimates using your script (only one stage of estimation needed), and they were very close to population values when standardizing the latent variables in the estimation (like they were in the population model).

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Dealing with endogeneity in lavaan
parts: Given your answer (thank you for taking the time), the problem must be that I am using the wrong estimation script:

Nothing wrong in your script.  You only estimate once (when you fit the analysis model to the data).  I ran the same script you posted, but I set the std.lv argument to TRUE:

mFit_NORM <- sem(mModel, data = mData_NORM, std.lv = TRUE)

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Dealing with endogeneity in lavaan
parts:
Thanks Terry. Just to be sure, I changed a bit my script and model specs., and used the "std.lv=TRUE" as you suggested:

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

library("lavaan", lib.loc="~/R/win-library/3.2")

# define Pop model

mPopModel <- '  
# outer model

CO =~ CO1
EU =~ 0.8*EU1 + 0.8*EU2 + 0.8*EU3 + 0.8*EU4 + 0.8*EU5

GT =~ 0.6*GT1 + 0.6*GT2 + 0.7*GT3 + 0.7*GT4 + 0.8*GT5
AC =~ 0.5*AC1 + 0.6*AC2 + 0.6*AC3 + 0.7*AC4 + 0.7*AC5
SU =~ 0.55*SU1 + 0.6*SU2 + 0.65*SU3 + 0.7*SU4 + 0.75*SU5
# inner model

EU ~ 0.418*CO
GT ~ 0.515*CO
AC ~ 0.288*CO
SU ~ 0.0*CO + 0.157*EU + 0.542*GT + 0.254*AC
'

# generate data based on Pop model
mData <- simulateData(mPopModel,sample.nobs=10000L,
                      standardized=TRUE)

# define analysis model

mModel <- '  
# outer model

CO =~ CO1
EU =~ EU1 + EU2 + EU3 + EU4 + EU5

GT =~ GT1 + GT2 + GT3 + GT4 + GT5
AC =~ AC1 + AC2 + AC3 + AC4 + AC5

SU =~ SU1 + SU2 + SU3 + SU4 + SU5
# inner model
EU ~ CO

GT ~ CO
AC ~ CO

SU ~ CO + EU + GT + AC
'

# analyze data
mFit <- sem(mModel,data=mData,std.lv=TRUE)
summary(mFit,nd=4,standardized=T,fit.measures=T,rsquare=T) # show std solution

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Still, I got results similar to the ones I had before - in terms of messed up estimates. For example:

Regressions:
                    Estimate   Std.Err   Z-value   P(>|z|)    Std.lv   Std.all
  EU ~                                                                        
    CO                0.2712    0.0107   25.3166    0.0000    0.2617    0.2617
  GT ~                                                                        
    CO                0.3455    0.0112   30.8270    0.0000    0.3266    0.3266
  AC ~                                                                        
    CO                0.1943    0.0115   16.9057    0.0000    0.1907    0.1907
  SU ~                                                                        
    CO                0.0307    0.0154    1.9881    0.0468    0.0210    0.0210
    EU                0.2690    0.0148   18.1983    0.0000    0.1909    0.1909
    GT                0.8411    0.0200   41.9680    0.0000    0.6094    0.6094
    AC                0.3686    0.0168   21.9949    0.0000    0.2571    0.2571

Looking at the values under the Std.lv column, the following regressions are too far off the true values: EU ~ CO,  GT ~ CO, and  AC ~ CO.

With a sample size of 10K, these regressions should be a lot closer to the true values than they are. That is what motivated my original post.

Now, I think you are correct that this is not due to endogeneity, because the analysis model is correctly specified vis-a-vis the population model. 

Maybe something missing in the settings of the sem() function, in addition to the "std.lv=TRUE" you mentioned?

Ned

Hi,

If you do

mData <- simulateData(mPopModel,sample.nobs=10000L,
                      standardized=TRUE, debug = TRUE)


You will get a lot of debugging information for data generation including the population values after standardization. These do not look correct:

50 50  CO ~~  CO    0     1    0 1.0000000   0        .p50.
51 51  EU ~~  EU    0     1    0 1.0000000   0        .p51.
52 52  GT ~~  GT    0     1    0 1.0000000   0        .p52.
53 53  AC ~~  AC    0     1    0 1.0000000   0        .p53.
54 54  SU ~~  SU    0     1    0 0.4424239   0        .p54.

Only CO is exogenous, so I would expect the variances of all other variables to be adjusted. But for some reason this does not happen. This may be a bug in the data generation code. 

Mikko

On 11/21/2015 08:57 PM, Ned Kock wrote:
> simulateData(mPopModel,sample.nobs=10000L,std.lv=TRUE,standardized=TRUE)

I would recommend to avoid using std.lv=TRUE and standardized=TRUE in
more complicated models (the two options interfere).

I would specify *all* population parameters, including the residual
variances.

Yves.
